topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European digital public health contexts; may not fully capture competency needs in other regions or non-health sectors, though frameworks have potential transferability.
takeaways: Identifies specific competency clusters needed for digital health roles; use to benchmark which AI and digital literacy skills your health or public sector organisation should prioritise in training programs.
European frameworks may differ from Australian health workforce standards — cross-reference with local AHPRA or state health department competency expectations before implementing recommendations.

Scoping review synthesises existing frameworks rather than testing new training interventions — useful for mapping the landscape but supplement with local needs analysis before rolling out capability development.

articles.title: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on dental education context; findings may not transfer directly to other professional disciplines or organisational settings without adaptation.
takeaways: Use a structured competency framework approach (rather than ad-hoc training) when introducing AI literacy to professional students; this allows you to map specific skills, knowledge areas, and attitudes systematically across your curriculum or workforce programme.

Tailor AI literacy competencies to your discipline's practical needs — in this case, dentistry's clinical workflows — so employees see direct relevance and can apply learning to real work scenarios rather than treating AI as generic IT knowledge.

Establish clear learning outcomes and assessment criteria upfront when designing AI capability programmes, ensuring both educators and learners understand what 'AI literacy' means in your specific professional context.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context; geographic scope and whether findings are based on empirical data or conceptual framework not clear from snippet alone. Applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development uncertain.
takeaways: Consider how AI competencies can be embedded within broader digital literacy frameworks rather than taught in isolation — this holistic approach may improve retention and transfer to real-world contexts.
Middle school is a critical window for foundational AI literacy; early exposure to AI concepts and competencies may build confidence and capability for adult learners later in their careers.

articles.title: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies - Sage Journals
articles.snippet: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies  Sage Journals
articles.generalisability: Limited — the snippet provides insufficient detail on geographic scope, sample characteristics, or methodology. The focus on Generation Z and educational strategies suggests primarily academic context, but applicability to workplace AI literacy programmes cannot be assessed from this information.
takeaways: Generation Z workforce entry requires educational institutions to embed AI literacy early, suggesting organisations should consider partnering with educational providers or designing onboarding programmes that don't assume prior AI knowledge.

Innovative educational strategies mentioned likely include hands-on, project-based learning — consider translating these into workplace upskilling through experiential AI tasks rather than lecture-based training.
The framing of 'skills gap' suggests identifying which specific AI competencies your organisation needs most, then designing targeted development pathways rather than generic AI awareness courses.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on public health faculty development; findings may not generalise to other disciplines or organisational contexts without further validation.
takeaways: Faculty development programs can shift mindsets from AI resistance to readiness; design programs that address misconceptions and provide hands-on experience rather than theory alone.

AI literacy in professional fields requires tailored curricula for domain-specific applications — public health educators need training in health-specific AI tools and use cases to credibly teach others.
Institutional readiness matters: change initiatives must address both individual capability and organisational support structures to sustain AI literacy adoption among staff.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on higher education sector which may not directly transfer to corporate workplace settings, but principles around competency development frameworks are broadly applicable.
takeaways: Identify which AI competencies are most relevant to your organisation's roles and develop targeted curricula or learning pathways rather than generic AI literacy programs.
Use a structured competency framework (technical, critical thinking, domain knowledge) to guide employee development—higher education models can be adapted for workplace contexts.
Create multi-modal learning opportunities combining theory, hands-on practice, and real-world application to build sustainable AI capabilities across your workforce.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — unable to assess sample size, geographic scope, or sector specificity from title and abstract fragment provided.
takeaways: Psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) appears to be a key mediator in how employees benefit from AI as a job resource rather than experiencing it as a threat — consider assessing and developing these capacities when implementing AI tools.
Framing AI as a job resource (augmentation, skill enhancement) rather than a replacement tool may unlock innovation outcomes; align messaging and change management accordingly.

Employee innovation in algorithm-driven roles depends partly on psychological capital — organisations should invest in building confidence, adaptive capacity, and goal-directed thinking alongside technical AI training.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are limited by focus on paternalistic leadership contexts, which are more common in Asian organizations; applicability to Western egalitarian leadership models requires further investigation.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools by involving employees in customizing or 'crafting' AI systems to suit their specific workflows — this increases collaboration and reduces resistance to AI adoption.
Paternalistic leaders should frame AI integration as a collaborative process where employees have agency in how tools are adapted and implemented, rather than top-down deployment.
Build psychological ownership early: employees who feel they have shaped or contributed to AI implementation are more likely to engage productively with the technology.

articles.title: Employees Are Relying on AI for Personal Support. That’s Risky. - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Employees Are Relying on AI for Personal Support. That’s Risky.  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a perspective piece reflecting general workplace trends rather than empirical research. Likely reflects North American/Western organisational contexts but geographic scope is not explicit.
takeaways: Monitor whether employees are using AI tools (ChatGPT, etc.) for emotional support or personal advice, as this may mask underlying wellbeing issues that organisations should address directly.

Establish clear guidelines on appropriate AI use in the workplace, particularly around personal matters, to mitigate risks of over-reliance, privacy breaches, and reduced help-seeking from actual support services.

Create accessible mental health and professional development resources so employees feel supported by human colleagues and managers rather than turning to AI as a substitute for interpersonal connection.

articles.title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — theoretical framework based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox; generalisability depends on empirical validation across different organisational contexts, sectors, and employee roles.
takeaways: Generative AI can trigger competing dynamics: automation (reducing need for certain knowledge skills) and augmentation (enhancing employee capability) — leaders must actively design workflows to maximise augmentation benefits while mitigating deskilling risks.

Monitor employee knowledge behaviours as AI adoption increases; watch for reduced knowledge-sharing, learning plateaus, or over-reliance on AI outputs, which may indicate automation effects outweighing augmentation gains.

Create deliberate practices (e.g., knowledge audits, peer review processes, documented reasoning) to ensure employees remain engaged in deep thinking and knowledge development rather than passively accepting AI-generated outputs.

articles.title: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — snippet provides insufficient detail on study design, sample size, geography, and methodology to assess generalisability. Full article review needed to evaluate whether findings apply beyond specific sector or organisation type.
takeaways: Prioritise psychological safety initiatives when implementing AI tools — workers who feel safe to speak up, take interpersonal risks, and ask for help are less likely to experience depression during AI adoption.
Monitor mental health outcomes during AI rollout, particularly for workers in low-psychological-safety environments; early intervention may prevent depression and disengagement.

Beyond technical AI training, invest in team norms and leader behaviours that create psychological safety — this appears to be a critical buffer against negative psychological effects of workplace AI.

articles.title: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — specific sample and sector not detailed in snippet; findings on job stress, AI self-efficacy, and cybersecurity behaviour may not generalise broadly without knowing participant demographics, organisational context, or geographic location.
takeaways: Build AI self-efficacy in cybersecurity roles as a protective factor — employees with higher confidence in their ability to work with AI show stronger security behaviours even under high job stress.

Address job stress as a barrier to safe cybersecurity practices — organisations should assess workload and pressure in security-critical roles, as stress may undermine even well-trained employees' adherence to protocols.

Tailor AI upskilling programmes to reduce uncertainty — structured training that builds genuine capability (not just confidence) can buffer employees against the stress that often accompanies rapid AI adoption in sensitive areas like cybersecurity.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner perspective on change management approaches, likely drawing on client engagements across multiple sectors, but specific sample details and geographic scope not provided in snippet.
takeaways: Shift framing from 'AI adoption' (a one-time implementation) to 'AI adaptation' (ongoing behavioral evolution) to align change strategies with the reality that effective AI use requires sustained habit formation and mindset shifts, not just tool rollout.

Design change interventions around building specific human behaviors needed for AI success (e.g., comfort with ambiguity, collaboration with AI systems, critical evaluation of outputs) rather than assuming technical training alone will drive capability development.

Use a structured change approach that accounts for behavioral resistance and capability gaps—moving beyond awareness campaigns to targeted, iterative support that addresses how people actually work with AI in context.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be an opinion piece or overview from a Stanford business school perspective, without clear empirical data or specified geographic scope. Findings may reflect primarily US business context and elite institution viewpoint.
takeaways: Identify which routine tasks in your team could be automated or augmented by AI, then plan explicit upskilling conversations with affected employees to reframe their roles toward higher-value work.

Design change management processes that address employee concerns about job displacement by showing concrete examples of how AI tools amplify (rather than replace) human expertise in your specific sector.
Create opportunities for employees to experiment with AI tools in low-stakes settings before full deployment, reducing anxiety and building confidence in new ways of working.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from title and snippet alone — the full article methodology would clarify sample size, geographic scope, and sector representation.
takeaways: AI adoption can trigger either approach behaviours (employees proactively redesigning tasks to complement AI) or avoidance behaviours (withdrawing from AI-affected work); understanding which pathway employees take helps tailor change management to encourage proactive adaptation rather than resistance.

Job crafting interventions may be more effective during AI rollouts than passive communication — explicitly inviting employees to reshape their roles and responsibilities around new AI tools can shift mindset from threat to opportunity.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on BCG's consulting experience across clients, but lacks transparent methodology, sample size disclosure, or peer review. Findings may reflect clients served by a US-headquartered consulting firm and may not represent all industry sectors equally.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability-building initiative rather than solely a technology implementation—this shifts how leaders communicate change and where they invest resources.

Identify and address the specific skill gaps and role transitions your workforce will face before rolling out AI tools, rather than implementing technology first and managing talent consequences reactively.

Design change management and training interventions that treat AI adoption as a behaviour change challenge requiring clear incentives, feedback loops, and opportunity to practise—not just technical training.

articles.title: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings are specific to Chinese primary and secondary school contexts. Cultural attitudes toward AI, educational systems, and teacher autonomy differ significantly from Australian schools, limiting direct transferability. Results may not generalise to other regions with different institutional structures or teacher demographics.
takeaways: AI adoption among educators is not uniformly positive — framing AI as a 'threat' to autonomy or job security can suppress innovative teaching behaviours, while framing it as a 'challenge' to develop skills encourages adoption. Monitor how AI is positioned in your change messaging.

Teachers' perception of control matters more than AI capability itself. Support staff in feeling they maintain pedagogical agency (e.g., choosing when and how to use AI tools) rather than being replaced, to sustain behaviour change toward innovation.

Consider individual differences in threat perception — some teachers may need targeted psychological support or skills development to shift from defensive to growth-oriented mindsets about AI integration.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey insights are based on client work and industry trends, but specific case examples and organisational contexts may not directly transfer to all Australian workplace settings.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling as organisational change management, not just technical training — this shifts focus from individual capability gaps to systemic transformation and change readiness.

Address resistance and mindset shifts as prerequisites to technical learning; employees need clarity on how AI roles will evolve and what job security looks like before they'll engage with upskilling.
Design upskilling programmes that connect to business outcomes and individual career pathways, making the 'why' explicit so employees understand personal relevance alongside organisational need.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: The surprising disconnect between intense romance and a couple’s sex life - PsyPost
articles.snippet: The surprising disconnect between intense romance and a couple’s sex life  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline finding requires access to underlying research to assess sample size, methodology, and cultural context. News reports typically lack methodological detail needed to evaluate broader applicability.
takeaways: Romantic intensity and sexual frequency operate on different tracks in relationships — passion doesn't automatically translate to more or better sex, which challenges the common assumption that love and desire move in lockstep.

The counterintuitive finding that romance and sexuality can disconnect reminds us that relationship dynamics are more nuanced than popular culture suggests, and couples shouldn't assume their emotional connection predicts their physical intimacy.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited information available from title and snippet alone; generalisability depends on sample size, participant demographics, and experimental design, which cannot be assessed from the provided text.
takeaways: People don't all remember surprising moments equally well — personality traits shape whether unexpected events stick in your memory or fade away.
This challenges the common assumption that shock or surprise alone makes memories vivid; individual differences matter just as much as the event itself.
It's counterintuitive that your personality could be a stronger predictor of what you remember than how shocking something was.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline-driven news report with insufficient methodological detail to assess sample size, geographic scope, or study design. Actual research quality and applicability unknown without access to the original study.
takeaways: Brain imaging can detect structural or functional differences in individuals with psychopathic traits, suggesting neurobiology plays a measurable role in personality variation.
The 'shocking difference' framing reflects media sensationalism — neurological differences are common across personality types, but headlines often overstate what the science actually shows.
Psychopathy exists on a spectrum and brain differences don't determine destiny; many people with similar neural patterns don't exhibit harmful behaviour, and environment and choice still matter.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — the underlying research source and sample characteristics are not provided, limiting assessment of how broadly findings apply.
takeaways: Antagonistic narcissism (dominance, assertiveness, low empathy) appears to carry short-term romantic appeal, likely due to confidence and boldness in pursuit.
This finding is counterintuitive because narcissism typically predicts relationship dysfunction — suggesting a mismatch between what initially attracts us and what sustains partnerships.
The research hints at a potential evolutionary or psychological puzzle: traits that seem attractive in early courtship may damage intimacy and trust over time.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — sample size, geographic scope, and methodology not specified. Findings may reflect patterns in English-language wine reviews or a specific wine review platform.
takeaways: Language patterns in wine reviews—like descriptive vocabulary and emotional tone—can reveal underlying personality traits, suggesting our writing style leaks personal characteristics even in niche domains like wine tasting.
AI can uncover hidden psychological signals in everyday consumer behaviour that humans might overlook, opening curious questions about what our leisure choices reveal about us.
Wine reviewing provides a fun window into personality expression: whether you're effusive, precise, emotional, or technical in tasting notes may say more about you than about the wine itself.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Likely broad — Cambridge research on global music preferences suggests findings across diverse populations, though specific sample composition and size not detailed in snippet.
takeaways: People with similar personalities gravitate toward the same music genres worldwide, suggesting personality shapes taste more than culture does.
Your Spotify playlist might actually be a personality fingerprint — what you listen to reveals consistent psychological patterns that transcend geography and language.
Music preference is a surprisingly universal signal: the same personality traits predict what someone enjoys listening to whether they're in Melbourne, Mumbai, or Mexico City.

topics.label: Psychological Safety

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — snippet provides insufficient detail on sample size, geography, methodology, and sector coverage to assess generalisability. Full article review needed.
takeaways: Psychological capital (confidence, hope, resilience, optimism) may be a key lever for helping employees view AI as a tool that enhances rather than threatens their work — consider assessing and developing these capacities in teams adopting AI systems.

Creating psychological safety around AI adoption may require deliberate attention to building employee optimism and resilience about algorithmic change, not just addressing surface-level fears about job loss.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.sample: Academic teams (geographic scope not specified in snippet)
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on multicultural academic teams; findings may not generalise to other sectors (corporate, public service, etc.) or non-diverse team contexts. Sample characteristics and size unclear from snippet.
takeaways: Explore how AI tools can help leaders identify and interrupt gendered patterns in team participation and decision-making — algorithmic flagging of whose voices are being heard may create accountability for inclusive behaviours.

Use AI-assisted leadership feedback to surface blind spots in your own inclusive leadership practice, particularly around which team members you're calling on or crediting in meetings — this data-driven reflection can shift behaviour more effectively than intuition alone.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad reach across multiple countries, though sampling methodology, response rates, and sector representation are not detailed in the snippet provided. Findings likely reflect perspectives of PwC's accessible workforce populations rather than the global workforce comprehensively.
takeaways: Use survey data on workforce concerns to benchmark psychological safety priorities within your organisation — identify whether your team's top fears align with or diverge from global patterns to target interventions effectively.

Translate global 'hopes' insights into specific safety initiatives: if data reveals shared desires (e.g. for autonomy, inclusion, or fair treatment), design team practices that visibly address these concerns to build trust.

Conduct a follow-up pulse survey within your own workforce to test whether PwC's global findings resonate locally — this grounds external benchmarks in your organisation's actual culture and psychology.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The mechanism linking AI adoption to depression through psychological safety and ethical leadership is theoretically sound but findings may be context-dependent — caution warranted until full methodology is reviewed.
takeaways: When introducing AI systems, prioritise creating psychological safety by involving employees early, inviting concerns without fear of repercussion, and transparently addressing anxieties about job security or role change.

Model and reinforce ethical AI use by leaders — employees' mental health outcomes may depend less on AI adoption itself than on whether leadership demonstrates responsible, trustworthy use and clear values alignment.

Monitor employee wellbeing proactively during AI transitions; depression signals may indicate insufficient psychological safety or perceived ethical lapses, not AI itself, so address root causes in leadership and team culture.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Limited — BCG report lacks detail on study methodology, sample composition, or geographic scope, making it difficult to assess how findings apply beyond the organizations studied.
takeaways: Create explicit norms that invite diverse perspectives and challenge without fear of retaliation; this levels participation and decision-making across hierarchy and seniority levels.
Measure psychological safety regularly through employee surveys and focus groups, then track whether inclusive behaviours and equal voice in meetings actually improve over time.
Leaders must model vulnerability and receptiveness to dissent first — employees watch whether senior staff genuinely welcome criticism before they'll contribute their own concerns or ideas.

articles.title: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams - SHRM
articles.snippet: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams  SHRM
articles.generalisability: Moderate — SHRM guidance reflects US HR practices and cultural contexts; principles may translate to Australian workplaces but should be adapted for local employment law, cultural norms, and organisational structures.
takeaways: Identify which of the four leadership practices your team leaders currently use inconsistently, and design targeted coaching or team workshops to strengthen the weakest area.

Measure baseline psychological safety in your teams (e.g. via pulse surveys asking whether people feel safe speaking up, asking questions, or admitting mistakes) and track changes quarterly after implementing leader behaviour changes.

Create explicit team norms around the behaviours that build safety — e.g. 'we assume good intent', 'mistakes are learning opportunities' — and have leaders model and reinforce these visibly in meetings and one-on-ones.
